Traveling Mercies
TRAV-uh-ling MUR-seez
noun phrase
A prayer idiom, especially common in American evangelical and older revival speech, asking God's protection and providence over a journey. The plural 'mercies' echoes the Authorized Version's frequent plural — 'the multitude of thy tender mercies' (Ps. 51:1) — and names the many small providences a traveler needs.

Neutral
A harmless and apt prayer idiom for safe travel; quaint, and worth praying in earnest rather than rattling off by reflex.

📖 Biblical Definition

To pray for safety in travel is thoroughly scriptural; the believer commits his journeys to God as he commits all his ways. 'In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths' (Prov. 3:6); 'The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore' (Ps. 121:8). Ezra 'proclaimed a fast... that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way for us, and for our little ones' (Ezra 8:21) — an Old Testament prayer for traveling mercies in all but the name. Paul longed to come to Rome 'by the will of God' (Rom. 1:10) and was kept through shipwreck and storm by the God who said 'Fear not, Paul' (Acts 27:24). The mercies themselves are real and daily: 'It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed... they are new every morning' (Lam. 3:22-23). 'Traveling mercies,' simply, asks the God of all our ways to keep us on this one.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A harmless and even apt prayer idiom for safe travel; mildly quaint and easily rattled off, but rightly meant it commits the journey to the God who preserves our going out and coming in (Ps. 121:8).

TRAVELING MERCIES, noun phrase. The protection and providence of God sought over a journey.

A prayer idiom of American evangelical and revival speech; the plural 'mercies' follows the Authorized Version's usage (Ps. 51:1; Lam. 3:22).

Apt sense: the believer committing his journeys to God, as Ezra sought 'a right way' (Ezra 8:21) and Paul travelled 'by the will of God' (Rom. 1:10).

Cautioned sense: reduced to a parting pleasantry rattled off without faith — a quaint farewell rather than a real petition to the God who keeps the way.

📖 Key Scripture

Psalm 121:8 — "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore."

Proverbs 3:6 — "In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths."

Ezra 8:21 — "Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river of Ahava, that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way for us, and for our little ones, and for all our substance."

Lamentations 3:22-23 — "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."

Acts 27:24 — "Saying, Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

No corruption to name — only the gentle danger of a worn idiom: 'traveling mercies' rattled off as a parting pleasantry, the words emptied of the faith that ought to fill them.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; it is a wholesome prayer-idiom, and the only caution is sincerity. 'Traveling mercies' simply asks God to keep a journey, which Scripture everywhere invites — 'commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass' (Ps. 37:5). There is nothing to recover from the world here. The one quiet danger is the danger of all familiar Christian speech: that a real petition hardens into a reflex, a parting word said as automatically as 'goodbye,' so that the lips move toward heaven while the heart stays on the curb. The Lord warned against 'vain repetitions' and lips that 'draw near me with their mouth... but have removed their heart far from me' (Matt. 6:7; Isa. 29:13).

The phrase can also drift toward a vague good-luck wish, as though 'mercies' were an impersonal fortune one hopes attends the road rather than the personal kindness of a personal God. But biblical mercy is never luck; it is the covenant chesed of the LORD, 'new every morning' (Lam. 3:23), given by Him who 'shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in' (Ps. 121:8). To ask for traveling mercies is to ask Someone for something, not to toss a coin into the air. Where the phrase loses that personal address, it loses the very thing that makes it prayer.

The recovery is small and glad: pray it meaningfully. When you ask traveling mercies for a friend, mean the God to whom you ask it — ask Him to direct the path (Prov. 3:6), to give a right way (Ezra 8:21), to bring the traveler safe to his coming in (Ps. 121:8), and to use the journey for His glory and the traveler's good. A worn idiom prayed in earnest is not vain repetition but a true and tender request, and the God of all mercies delights to hear it.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

A prayer idiom for safe travel, mildly quaint but rightly meant; biblical mercy is the LORD's personal chesed, new every morning (Lam. 3:22-23), not impersonal luck. Pray it in earnest, not by reflex.

English: an evangelical/revival prayer idiom; the plural 'mercies' follows the Authorized Version (Ps. 51:1; Lam. 3:22).

Hebrew: the LORD's chesed, covenant mercy and lovingkindness — personal kindness, never impersonal fortune.

Biblical pattern: Ezra 8:21 and Ps. 121:8 — the journey committed to the God who preserves the going out and coming in.

Usage

"She asked traveling mercies for the family on the road, and meant it — a real petition to the God who keeps the going out and coming in."

"A worn idiom prayed in earnest is not vain repetition; the danger is only the reflex that moves the lips while the heart stays on the curb."

"Mercy is not luck; it is the LORD's lovingkindness, new every morning — ask Someone for it, do not toss it to the wind."
